items.title: 15.5.1 Central Nervous System - Brain & Spinal Cord

source_refs.note: Topic 15.5.1 with its Tidbits and For Information boxes (PDF 36-40); Figures 15.9 to 15.14 are replaced by original diagrams.

blocks.text: The CNS is made of inter-neurons and neuroglia. The brain lies in the cranium and the spinal cord in the vertebral column, and both are covered by three protective membranes, the meninges.

items: Dura mater: the outermost, thick layer just below the skull and vertebrae, containing the larger blood vessels.
Arachnoid: a thin second layer that acts as a barrier between the cerebrospinal fluid below it and the blood in the dura mater.
Pia mater: a very delicate third layer that sticks to the surface of the brain and spinal cord; its capillaries nourish them.

blocks.alt: A curved section through the top of the head showing, from outside in, the skull, the dura mater, the thin arachnoid, the space between the arachnoid and the pia mater with its web-like strands, the pia mater and the brain tissue.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.9: The meninges of brain (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.9).

blocks.text: The average adult brain weighs about 1.4 kg (about 2% of body weight) and contains about 100 billion inter-neurons, each with synapses to several thousand others. In Grade X the brain was studied by its traditional divisions, forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain; here it is described by its latest defined divisions.

blocks.alt: Mid-line section of the brain inside the cranium. The folded cerebrum arches over the corpus callosum; below it are the lateral ventricles, the third ventricle, the thalamus and hypothalamus (diencephalon) and the pituitary gland. The midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata (brainstem) lead down to the spinal cord, with the cerebellum behind and the fourth ventricle between them.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.10: Major parts of human brain (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.10).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Lateral ventricles, Third ventricle, Cranium (Skull), Pituitary gland, Fourth ventricle, Cerebrum, Corpus callosum, Thalamus and Hypothalamus (bracketed Diencephalon), Midbrain, Pons and Medulla oblongata (bracketed Brainstem), Cerebellum, Spinal cord.

items: Cerebrum: the largest part, its outer layer highly folded. A deep fissure divides it into left and right cerebral hemispheres, joined at the base of the fissure by the corpus callosum, a band of axons. Each hemisphere receives sensation from, and sends motor commands to, the opposite side of the body.

Brainstem, below the cerebrum and joining it to the spinal cord: the midbrain relays visual and auditory information and contains the reticular formation; the pons carries impulses between the cerebral hemispheres and the cerebellum; the medulla oblongata is a relay and control centre for heart rate, breathing and other homeostatic activities.

Diencephalon, deep in the centre above the brainstem: the thalamus relays sensory information to the cerebrum; the hypothalamus integrates visceral activities, regulates body temperature, hunger and satiety, thirst and emotions, and controls the pituitary gland.

Cerebellum, below and behind the cerebral hemispheres: a tightly folded cortex over white matter; it receives impulses from muscles, tendons, joints, eyes and ears, controls posture and coordinates rapid movements together with the brainstem and cerebral cortex.

blocks.text: The limbic system is a group of linked structures on both sides of the thalamus, under the cerebrum: the hypothalamus, the two almond-shaped amygdalae deep in the temporal lobes (love, hate, anger, fear, rage and sexual arousal), and the hippocampus, two horns curving back from the amygdalae, which moves information from short-term into long-term memory. The pineal gland, where the two halves of the thalamus join, makes melatonin, which controls sleep patterns.

blocks.alt: Mid-line section of the brain showing the limbic system: the hypothalamus (green) below the front of the thalamus, the almond-shaped amygdala deep in the temporal lobe (circled), and the hippocampus curving back from it, with the fornix arching over the thalamus.

blocks.text: Ridges on the hemispheres are gyri, separated by shallow grooves (sulci) and deep grooves (fissures). The folded outer layer, the cerebral cortex, is grey matter packed with inter-neurons. Its motor areas send impulses to skeletal muscles; its sensory areas receive information, the auditory cortex in the temporal lobe dealing with sound frequencies and the visual cortex in the occipital lobe with information from the eyes; its association areas carry out higher mental activities, some on one side, such as language on the left and visual-spatial ability on the right. Below the cortex lies white matter of myelinated axons linking the regions. Damage to one hemisphere causes loss of sensation and paralysis on the opposite side of the body.

blocks.alt: Side view of a cerebral hemisphere, front to the right, coloured by area: primary motor area (pink strip) in front of the primary sensory area (blue strip); somatic association area in the front part; somatic sensory and association area behind the sensory strip; visual association area and visual area at the back; auditory cortex (yellow) in the temporal lobe with the sensory area for speech at its back end; motor area for speech in front, near the motor strip.

blocks.text: The brain and spinal cord are hollow, with fluid-filled cavities called ventricles that produce and circulate cerebrospinal fluid. There are four: two large lateral ventricles in the cerebrum, the third ventricle in the diencephalon between the two halves of the thalamus, and the fourth between the cerebellum and brainstem, continuous with the central canal of the spinal cord.

The spinal cord is a cable of neurons running from the medulla oblongata down through the backbone, protected by the vertebral column and the meninges; it is 0.25 to 0.5 inch across, wider in the cervical region (arms and trunk) and the lumbar region (legs). Its grey and white matter are arranged the opposite way to the brain: an inner H- or butterfly-shaped zone of grey matter (cell bodies of inter-neurons and motor neurons, neuroglia, non-myelinated axons) round a central canal, and an outer zone of white matter (myelinated axons). It is the information highway between the body and the brain.

blocks.alt: Cross-section of the spinal cord with an H-shaped grey matter core in white matter, and on each side a dorsal root with a ganglion and a ventral root joining into a spinal nerve. A sensory neuron (pink) runs in from the receptors through the ganglion and dorsal root to an interneuron in the grey matter; a motor neuron (blue) runs out through the ventral root and spinal nerve to the effectors.
